name: The Kingdom of Aksum
title: Social Hierarchy of the Kingdom of Aksum: From King of Kings to Slave
in: the Kingdom of Aksum under Ezana

tiers.name: The king of kings
tiers.you: You call yourself king of the Aksumites and of peoples across the Red Sea, put your face on gold coins, and lead your armies against the Bega, with your brother as one of your commanders.
tiers.kid: King Ezana of Aksum put his picture on gold coins and became one of the first kings anywhere to take up Christianity.
tiers.rise: Tradition holds that Ezana succeeded his father Ella Amida (Ousanas) as a child, with his mother Sofya as regent. Stuart Munro-Hay thought that in the early kingdom a new king of kings may have been chosen from among all the kings of a confederacy rather than by birth order.
tiers.why: The ruler of Aksum called himself king of kings, a title often found in inscriptions, and in a Greek inscription Ezana named himself king of the Aksumites, the Himyarites, Reeidan, the Ethiopians, the Sabaites and…

tiers.name: Royal kin, nobles and lesser kings
tiers.you: You live in a great house of stone and timber in Aksum, and you expect to be buried in a stone coffin with your jewellery, under a stone carved with the mark of your rank.
tiers.kid: Aksum’s nobles were buried under tall carved stones that showed how important they were.
tiers.rise: Rank came with kinship to the king and with his favour: Sazanas, an army commander, was raised in Ezana’s later years to share his throne, and a Roman emperor’s letter of 356/57 was addressed to both brothers.
tiers.why: Below the king stood a small elite whose ranks the sources glimpse mainly through their buildings and graves.

tiers.name: Priests and the first clergy
tiers.you: You serve the faith King Ezana has taken up, under a bishop who was once a slave and whom a Roman emperor would like to see replaced.
tiers.kid: Aksum’s first bishop, Frumentius, had once been a slave. He taught the young king and helped him become a Christian.
tiers.rise: A bishop was appointed in contact with the Church of Alexandria, as Frumentius was. He had once been a slave, so the new church’s first leader rose from the bottom of the ladder.
tiers.why: Before Ezana’s conversion the Aksumites worshipped gods related to those of southern Arabia, among them Astar, Mahrem, Beher and Medr, under the sign of the disc and crescent; great stone monuments honoured kings and…

tiers.name: Merchants and foreign traders
tiers.you: You ship ivory and tortoiseshell from Adulis to Roman Egypt and India, deal with your partners in Greek, and are paid in the king’s gold coins.
tiers.kid: Merchants at Aksum’s port of Adulis traded ivory and gold for silk and spices from faraway lands.
tiers.rise: Trade and coined money belonged to the towns: most Aksumite coins are found in the large trading centres and very few in remote villages, where people traded by barter.
tiers.why: Aksum’s merchants worked the trade between the Mediterranean and India.

tiers.name: Farmers and herders
tiers.you: You plough terraced fields of teff and barley, keep cattle and goats, and trade by barter in your village, for the king’s coins rarely reach it.
tiers.kid: Most people in Aksum were farmers who grew a grain called teff and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
tiers.rise: Little is recorded of how farmers rose or fell. Ordinary people were buried without coffins, with a few grave goods: pottery, glassware and iron tools.
tiers.why: Most Aksumites lived by farming and herding in the highlands, where settlement was dense in northeastern Tigray and central Eritrea.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were brought to the coast with ivory and incense and are waiting at Adulis to be shipped across the sea.
tiers.kid: Some people in Aksum were enslaved and sold to traders from far away across the sea.
tiers.rise: Frumentius rose from slave and royal tutor to Bishop of Ethiopia around 330. For the slaves sold abroad through Adulis, no way back is recorded.
tiers.why: Slaves appear in the record of Aksum mostly as goods for sale.
